title: Clarinet player on the Hirt job and owner Dan Levy
summary: Unsure who the clarinetist was (Pete Fountain or Tony Costa); Netto recalls weekend-only work and Dan Levy keeping the club going despite poor crowds.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: You get to have a clarinet player?
Yeah, P. Fonten and ... Part of the hymn. And ... No, I'm ... Big tall fellow? Yeah, yeah. He plays a little out now.
Oh, you're thinking of ... Yeah, swing player. Tony DeFranco. Tony DeFranco. Tony Costa. Tony Costa.
I don't remember that. I really don't. Yeah, he was down there.

Yeah, he could have been, I just don't remember. Well, we only played down there Friday, Saturday, and Sunday. And they were playing a spot job crisis down there. And Dan, I was raised with Dan. I knew Dan from a kid up, Dan Levy. And I told him, I says, Dan, I says, we're not taking enough money to pay one person in the band. I said, how long are you going to take this beating? They'll come. Don't worry. They'll come. Dan was loaded, you know. And when he gets so, he'd get loaded and couldn't talk. He didn't talk. And he says, they'll be here. He says, you getting your money? Yeah. I said, yeah. I said, but after all, I said, you going to run out of money? He says, oh, so he kept on, kept on. Sure enough, they finally came. And, well, Jumbo, Jumbo, Jumbo, I told you, Jumbo, Pete, he put their brains in a head and he, well, before the mic, he'd fly backwards. We used to have that expression, the whistle through his ass. But he's a good guy. He's a good guy.
